summary: Defines EAP-AKA', a small revision of the EAP-AKA method with a new key derivation that binds keys to the access network name and uses SHA-256 instead of SHA-1. It also updates RFC 4187. This is an informational document, updated by RFC 9048 and RFC 9678.

plainLanguage.summary: EAP-AKA' is a revision of EAP-AKA that includes the access-network name when deriving keys. It uses SHA-256 and adds a mechanism to help detect attempts to force both sides onto EAP-AKA instead.

questions: how does eap-aka' differ from eap-aka
what is a bidding down attack in eap
subtitle: EAP-AKA' binds derived keys to an access-network name and uses SHA-256.

tldr.problem: EAP-AKA does not bind its derived keys to the access-network name, and the revised 3GPP key derivation needs an unambiguous way to be negotiated.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-AKA' uses a separate EAP method type, sends the network name, negotiates a key derivation function, and uses CK', IK', and SHA-256. An added EAP-AKA attribute helps detect downgrade attempts.
tldr.outcome: The method binds keys to a network name and updates RFC 4187 to prevent bidding-down attacks. RFC 5448 was updated by RFC 9048 and RFC 9678.

today: RFC 5448 is an Informational document that updates RFC 4187. It has itself been updated by RFC 9048 and RFC 9678.

sections.title: Why EAP-AKA' Exists
sections.content:
EAP-AKA' revises the EAP-AKA method defined in RFC 4187. Its key derivation uses the access-network name, which limits the usefulness of keys exposed by a compromised access-network node.

The change must be unambiguous so old and new equipment do not derive different keys without detecting an error. EAP-AKA' therefore has its own EAP method type, 50 rather than EAP-AKA's 23. It also uses SHA-256 instead of SHA-1.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP-AKA' includes the access-network name when deriving keys, which ties those keys to that network. It has a separate method number so the two versions are not confused.

sections.title: Sending and Checking the Network Name
sections.content:
The server sends the access-network name in the AT_KDF_INPUT attribute, type 23. The value contains a 2-byte name length and a UTF-8 name, padded with zero bytes when needed so the attribute length is a multiple of 4 bytes. The name must not be empty.

The peer may compare the received name with its own view of the network. If policy allows it to continue despite a mismatch, it must use the name received from the server. The server also sends AT_KDF values in preference order so the peer and server can agree on a supported key derivation function.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends a name for the access network, and the peer can compare it with what it observes. Both sides also agree on which key-derivation method to use.

sections.title: Deriving the Session Keys
sections.content:
For AT_KDF value 1, both sides derive the master key from IK', CK', the string EAP-AKA', and the peer identity using PRF'. They split the first 1664 output bits into K_encr, K_aut, K_re, MSK, and EMSK. CK' and IK' are derived using the network name supplied in AT_KDF_INPUT.

PRF' uses HMAC-SHA-256. AT_MAC uses HMAC-SHA-256-128, which keeps the first 16 bytes of the HMAC output. The server sets the AMF separation bit to 1, and the peer must check it. Fast reauthentication must not change the network name.
sections.plainLanguage: The method combines AKA key material with the network name and derives separate keys for encryption, authentication, and later use. It uses SHA-256-based calculations and checks an authentication bit before proceeding.

sections.title: Detecting a Downgrade to EAP-AKA
sections.content:
EAP method negotiation can be attacked by a man in the middle who tries to force weaker methods. RFC 5448 adds AT_BIDDING, type 136, to EAP-AKA messages. It signals that a sender supports and prefers EAP-AKA'. The attribute is protected by EAP-AKA integrity.

If the peer sees that both sides support and prefer EAP-AKA' but are using EAP-AKA, it fails authentication as if AUTN were incorrect. A peer that does not support EAP-AKA' ignores the attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: AT_BIDDING tells the peer that the server supports and prefers EAP-AKA'. If both sides could have used that method but are using EAP-AKA, the peer treats the exchange as a possible downgrade and fails it.

sections.title: What Network-Name Binding Protects
sections.content:
Under the RFC's assumption that SHA-256 is at least as secure as SHA-1, EAP-AKA' is at least as secure as EAP-AKA for several properties, including mutual authentication, replay protection, and dictionary-attack resistance. Network-name binding means leaked derived keys are useful only with that name.

This does not stop a compromised access point from representing itself. The benefit depends on how access-network names are assigned; if a name identifies only an access technology, keys may still be useful in other networks using the same technology. EAP-AKA' does not provide channel bindings as defined by EAP.
sections.plainLanguage: Network-name binding can limit where leaked keys work, but it cannot prevent a compromised access point from acting as itself. The protection also depends on how specifically networks are named.
